network.overall_strategy: This is an evidence-stratified candidate network, not a claim that ten independently validated prebiotic glutamine syntheses exist. Ten distinct route records are provided: six combine two glycine-supply options with three experimentally tested meteorite irradiation formulations; three reach the common aminodinitrile through different precursor histories but depend on one explicitly unresolved glutamine-forming hydrolysis; and one represents the provisional nitrate–pyruvate mineral result. The six irradiation routes are feedstock/formulation variants of one reported target-forming chemistry, not six independently established mechanisms. Glutamine and its aminodinitrile contain five carbons; no enantioselective synthesis is assumed. Simple boundary feedstocks are admitted without claiming their complete geological supply. Unsupported selective glutamate activation and multiple hypothetical hydrolysis-order variants are excluded. Critically, rxn_005–rxn_007 are empirical mixture-to-product observations with unknown coproducts: their stoichiometric coefficients cannot legitimately be inferred from the listed species, and missing products are not fabricated. Other explicitly identified lumped equations are hypotheses rather than measured mass balances. Reaction sequences are topological assembly plans and can include parallel precursor preparation. Proposed operating windows are distinguished from reported conditions. Acid–base equilibria are abbreviated; iron-ion nodes represent mineral redox inventories rather than freely dissolved ferric iron at alkaline pH. Formation must be followed by separation and cool, shaded storage, but no end-to-end yield, transport time, accumulation rate, or greater-than-0.90 confidence is supported by the supplied evidence.

reactions.name: HCN oligomerization supplying diaminomaleonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8–10 in a concentrated, shaded cyanide reservoir. The supplied report does not establish the required concentration, residence time, or environmental DAMN yield. HCN volatility and competing oligomerization must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Successive cyanide-derived C–C bond formation gives the HCN tetramer; DAMN is one product of a competing oligomerization network, not an exclusive product.
reactions.reasoning: Bizzarri et al. (2026) identify DAMN as an HCN-derived tetramer and use it as an input, but do not demonstrate this upstream preparation as part of their glutamine experiment. The environmental implementation and transfer into the irradiation mixture are therefore speculative. Shading limits further DAMN photochemistry before its intended use.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde Strecker synthesis of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8–9.5 with ammonia and cyanide available together. Concentrations and conversion time are not established by the supplied research; competing formaldehyde reactions are expected.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine/iminium equilibrium with formaldehyde; cyanide addition produces aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is classical Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850), with related prebiotic aldehyde–cyanide–ammonia chemistry supported by Fernández-García et al. (2017). The supplied findings do not establish this particular glycine-supply module under the proposed conditions, so its environmental integration is speculative rather than a demonstrated part of the glutamine synthesis.

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis to glycine

conditions.other: Proposed acidic processing at pH 1–3, followed by cooling, neutralization, and separation before irradiation. Neither a rate nor an environmental yield is supplied. This heating stage precedes glutamine formation.

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile hydrates through an amide and hydrolyzes to the carboxylic acid, releasing ammonia; glycine has no second nitrile requiring differential hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: Nitrile hydrolysis is the established finishing transformation of Strecker amino-acid synthesis (Strecker, 1850). Unlike the glutamine aminodinitrile, this substrate does not present an α-versus-side-chain hydrolysis problem. The specified prebiotic processing window and subsequent recovery are speculative integrations not demonstrated in the supplied glutamine studies.

reactions.name: Ferroan-brucite nitrate reduction coupled to glycine formation

conditions.temperature: Experimental value not provided in the supplied summary; no hot-vent temperature is inferred
conditions.pressure: Not specified in the supplied summary
conditions.catalyst: Ferroan brucite: consumable Fe(II) redox inventory, reactive surface, and adsorbent
conditions.other: Alkaline mineral interface; exact pH and time-dependent yield require the original study. Fe2+/Fe3+ and H+ are redox/proton bookkeeping references, not a claim of soluble ferric iron or acidic bulk solution. Acidic product recovery and removal of mineral residues are required before reuse.

reactions.mechanism: Mineral Fe(II) supplies reducing equivalents for nitrate reduction and carbonyl reductive amination. Formal electron balance requires ten Fe(II)-to-Fe(III) oxidations per glycine when nitrate is the nitrogen source; the mineral phase evolution is not resolved here.
reactions.reasoning: Chimiak et al. (2024) provide peer-reviewed evidence for glycine formation in the ferroan-brucite nitrate platform, unlike the earlier provisional glutamine claim. Up to 97% of newly formed glycine could remain mineral-bound until acid digestion. The experiment therefore supports production, but not automatic availability of dissolved glycine for another reaction. Natural extraction, concentration, and transfer into the radiation system remain unvalidated.

reactions.name: Reported glutamine detection after irradiation with Canyon Diablo material
agents: 1 wt% powdered Canyon Diablo iron meteorite

conditions.pressure: Not specified in the supplied report
conditions.catalyst: Canyon Diablo meteorite material; active phase and catalytic mechanism unresolved
conditions.other: Reported charge: formamide, DAMN, and glycine, 2.5 mmol each; 170 MeV protons, 6 Gy total dose, 3 min irradiation. This is a cold concentrated organic matrix, not a 300–370 K liquid surface pool. Anoxia is required by this model, but the experimental atmosphere must be checked in the original paper.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical mixture-to-product observation. Radiolytic radical and Strecker-like processes are proposed, but carbon/nitrogen atom mapping and coproducts are unresolved. This node is not a balanced elementary or overall reaction and must not be used for automatic stoichiometric inference.
reactions.reasoning: Bizzarri et al. (2026), as described in the supplied research, report glutamine identified after derivatization by GC–MS at 20.76 micrograms per milligram of crude residue after formamide removal. This is not a molar conversion yield or an isolated-product yield. The result supports direct analytical detection, not a resolved mechanism, prebiotic supply chain, natural proton exposure, or long-term accumulation.

reactions.name: Reported glutamine detection after irradiation with NWA 4482 material

conditions.pressure: Not specified in the supplied report
conditions.catalyst: NWA 4482 meteorite material; active phase and catalytic mechanism unresolved
conditions.other: Reported charge: formamide, DAMN, and glycine, 2.5 mmol each; 170 MeV protons, 6 Gy, 3 min. Non-bulk-aqueous cold matrix. Experimental gas atmosphere and compatibility with anoxic operation require verification.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical irradiation-product association with an unresolved multicomponent reaction network. Missing coproducts are deliberately not invented; the displayed species do not constitute a stoichiometrically closed equation.
reactions.reasoning: Bizzarri et al. (2026) report 9.86 micrograms glutamine per milligram crude residue with NWA 4482. The different mineral assemblage experimentally changes the product distribution, justifying a separate formulation node. It does not establish a distinct atom-resolved glutamine mechanism. Geochemical dose equivalence, precursor delivery, and product survival remain untested.

reactions.name: Reported glutamine detection after irradiation with Gold Basin material
agents: 1 wt% powdered Gold Basin chondritic meteorite

conditions.pressure: Not specified in the supplied report
conditions.catalyst: Gold Basin meteorite material; active phase and catalytic mechanism unresolved
conditions.other: Reported charge: formamide, DAMN, and glycine, 2.5 mmol each; 170 MeV protons, 6 Gy, 3 min. Cold concentrated matrix; pH is not meaningfully assigned as for an aqueous pool. The original experimental atmosphere is not specified in the supplied summary.

reactions.mechanism: Empirical mixture-to-glutamine observation, not a specified elementary mechanism. Atom mapping, unreported products, and the actual consumption ratios of starting components are unknown.
reactions.reasoning: Bizzarri et al. (2026) report 2.24 micrograms glutamine per milligram crude residue with Gold Basin material. This lower reported abundance is retained rather than assigning all meteorites a generic catalytic efficiency. The formulation is experimentally distinct, but its geological implementation and any complete route from the network feedstocks remain conditional.

reactions.name: Cu(II)-supported oxidative coupling to cyanoacetylene

conditions.temperature: 300–310 K, proposed surface window; exact experimental value not supplied
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm in the proposed surface setting
conditions.other: Separate this oxidative stage from sulfide-rich and Fe(II)-rich solutions. Two Cu(II) reductions supply the formal two-electron oxidation. No molecular oxygen or unprovided Cu(I) reoxidation cycle is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-mediated oxidative coupling joins acetylene and cyanide to form cyanoacetylene, with Cu(II) reduced to Cu(I). Ligand and acid–base speciation are abbreviated.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support copper-mediated access to cyanoacetylene, with greater than approximately 25% yield reported in the supplied summary. Under the imposed anoxic conditions, Cu(II) must be an available oxidant rather than an indefinitely regenerated catalyst. Its supply and survival in an Fe(II)-rich setting are substantial geochemical limitations, not solved by the equation.

reactions.name: Cyanide addition giving the maleonitrile branch

conditions.other: HCN/cyanide and ammonia delivered after cyanoacetylene preparation. Exact experimental pH is not supplied. This graph follows maleonitrile without claiming it is the exclusive dinitrile product.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition across the activated alkyne generates an unsaturated C4 dinitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report C4 dinitrile formation, including maleonitrile, from cyanoacetylene with cyanide and ammonia. Competing isomers and other products are possible. Sequential reagent delivery is retained because the cited network is not demonstrated as one compatible homogeneous mixture.

reactions.name: Sulfide-driven photoreduction of maleonitrile
agents: Copper cyanide complexes participating in photoredox chemistry

conditions.other: UV exposure with sulfide/HS− as electron donor; proposed near-neutral to mildly alkaline solution. The supplied summary does not establish the exact UV spectrum, fluence, copper loading, or exposure time.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical electron/proton transfer reduces the C=C bond. S8 is an idealized elemental-sulfur endpoint for balancing; actual sulfur products can include other sulfur species.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 90% conversion of the unsaturated dinitrile precursor to succinonitrile under their photochemical conditions. This step consumes sulfide reducing power and requires light; a mineral surface alone is not substituted for either. Copper precipitation and sulfur-product speciation constrain environmental transferability.

reactions.name: Selective photoreduction of succinonitrile to 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: Controlled UV exposure and sulfide supply followed by prompt cyanide trapping. Exact irradiation time, pH, and kinetic selectivity must be taken from the original experiment, not inferred from the reported yield.

reactions.mechanism: Partial reduction of one nitrile gives an imine-like intermediate whose hydrolysis releases ammonia and produces an aldehyde. The remaining nitrile is retained.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 89% access to the semialdehyde in the supplied account. This supports selective precursor formation under tested conditions, not glutamine formation. S8 again represents an idealized oxidized-sulfur balance rather than a complete measured sulfur inventory.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin trapping of 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: Rapid delivery of cyanide to the aldehyde-containing solution. Cyanide concentration, pH, and residence time control trapping relative to polymerization and competing addition.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the aldehyde carbonyl and protonation gives the C5 cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) describe essentially quantitative cyanohydrin formation under their conditions. Fernández-García et al. (2017) independently support efficient trapping in the acrolein-derived system. Neither result establishes that isolated semialdehyde must accumulate in a natural pool.

reactions.name: Strecker conversion of the cyanohydrin system to aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich solution; proposed pH 8–9.5 is a screening window, not a quoted optimum. Reaction monitoring must distinguish cyanohydrin, aldehyde, aminodinitrile, and polymeric products.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation feeds aldehyde–imine formation and cyanide capture. This is not assumed to be direct substitution of an unactivated hydroxyl group by ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 70% overall yield across cyanohydrin/aminonitrile formation in the supplied summary; Fernández-García et al. (2017) support the related acrolein-derived precursor route. The product is a five-carbon aminodinitrile, not free glutamine.

reactions.name: Unresolved selective aminodinitrile hydrolysis required for glutamine

conditions.temperature: No validated operating window; 290–310 K is only a proposed screening range
conditions.other: No demonstrated pH, catalyst, reaction time, or product distribution achieves the required discrimination. A proposed pH screen around 5.5–8.5 is not a recipe. Success requires measured glutamine formation exceeding hydrolysis, cyclization, and other losses.

reactions.mechanism: Formal required net transformation: the α-nitrile becomes a carboxyl group with ammonia release, while the side-chain nitrile stops at the amide. The sequence and selectivity mechanism are unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Explicitly speculative. Patel et al. (2015) and Fernández-García et al. (2017) support advanced precursor access, not a quantitatively closed selective conversion to free glutamine. No unsupported preference for α-first or terminal-first hydrolysis is assigned. This single gap node records the decisive bottleneck rather than multiplying unvalidated hydrolysis orders into purportedly independent syntheses.

reactions.name: Aldol/dehydration source of acrolein

conditions.other: Neutral-to-basic aqueous conditions. The cited work supports low steady-state acrolein, not accumulation at the concentration used in the downstream cyanide experiment. Evaporative concentration cannot be assumed to outrun acrolein loss.

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde-derived nucleophilic addition to formaldehyde gives a β-hydroxy aldehyde that dehydrates to acrolein.
reactions.reasoning: Cleaves (2003) reports low but measurable acrolein production from dilute formaldehyde and acetaldehyde. This supplies a chemically motivated upstream source, but its throughput into the concentrated Fernández-García et al. (2017) chemistry has not been demonstrated. Aldol side reactions and acrolein polymerization remain important competitors.

reactions.name: Coupled cyanide Michael addition and cyanohydrin capture of acrolein

conditions.other: Representative reported conditions: about 140 mM acrolein, 700 mM KCN, pH about 9.2. HCN is the graph's neutral formula reference for the HCN/CN− pool. These concentrations are experimental benchmarks, not established environmental abundances.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide first adds conjugatively to acrolein, generating transient 3-cyanopropanal; a second cyanide addition traps its aldehyde as the C5 cyanohydrin. The cyanide ID appears once, with its coefficient implicit.
reactions.reasoning: Fernández-García et al. (2017) report approximately 95% cyanohydrin formation under the summarized conditions. The observed endpoint is modeled directly, without asserting accumulation or isolation of 3-cyanopropanal in this experiment. High cyanide concentration and acrolein availability are unresolved geochemical constraints.

reactions.name: Discharge-generated acrolein source, represented by a schematic net equation

conditions.temperature: Nonequilibrium electrical discharge; bulk experimental temperature not supplied
conditions.other: Anoxic reducing-gas source followed by aqueous capture. The displayed methane/water equation is a formal source projection, not a reconstruction of the original gas recipe. Capture into a 300–310 K pool is a proposed transfer step.

reactions.mechanism: Energetic gas-phase fragmentation, carbon-chain growth, and oxygen incorporation can generate acrolein within a complex product mixture. Hydrogen is the formal redox-balancing coproduct; this equation is not an elementary mechanism or measured product mass balance.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump and Miller (1972) support acrolein formation in discharge chemistry. The supplied report does not provide sufficient experimental detail to assign the precise gas composition, yield, energy input, or delivery rate. Consequently, this particular net equation and its integration with cyanide trapping are explicitly speculative, while the general discharge source has experimental precedent.

reactions.name: Provisional ferroan-brucite nitrate–pyruvate route to glutamine

conditions.temperature: Not specified in the supplied conference summary
conditions.pressure: Not specified in the supplied conference summary
conditions.catalyst: Ferroan brucite: reactive mineral and consumable Fe(II) reductant
conditions.other: Reported substrate ranges: 1–250 mM pyruvate and nitrate; durations: 2 days to 14 months. Numerical pH and the conditions corresponding to the maximum glutamine result are not supplied. Formal H+ and iron-ion nodes do not imply acidic bulk fluid or soluble Fe(III).

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized surface C–C chemistry, carbon loss, nitrogen reduction, and amidation. The displayed decarboxylative net projection uses two pyruvates per glutamine and fourteen Fe(II) oxidations; neither that atom mapping nor CO2 as the actual lost-carbon product has been demonstrated.
reactions.reasoning: Chimiak et al. (2023, Goldschmidt conference abstract) report up to approximately 1% glutamine. This remains provisional, not a peer-reviewed mechanistic demonstration. Chimiak et al. (2024) validate related glycine/3-hydroxyaspartate chemistry, not this glutamine assignment. The CO2-containing net equation is explicitly a testable hypothesis motivated by the proposed carbon-loss mechanism. Isotope tracing, full product balance, mineral characterization, and glutamine synthesis-versus-decay measurements are still required.

reactions.name: Competing glutamine side-chain deamidation

conditions.temperature: 300–370 K, environmental exposure range rather than a measured kinetic window
conditions.other: Rates depend strongly on temperature and pH. No rate constant or storage lifetime is available from the supplied excerpts. This sink must be measured during any proposed accumulation experiment.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the side-chain carboxamide produces glutamate and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied report identifies glutamine hydrolysis as a preservation problem but does not give author/year metadata for the underlying decomposition studies. The reaction is standard amide chemistry; its rate under this network's conditions is explicitly unvalidated. Bizzarri et al. (2026) provide an endpoint detection, not the synthesis-versus-degradation kinetics needed to establish accumulation.

reactions.name: Competing glutamine cyclization to pyroglutamate

conditions.temperature: 300–370 K, with warmer exposure expected to increase loss
conditions.other: Intramolecular cyclization can compete during storage and thermal processing. No validated lifetime, protective mineral effect, or permissible transport time is supplied. Avoid routing formed glutamine through the heated precursor-preparation stage.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack of the α-amino group on the side-chain amide carbonyl forms a five-membered lactam with ammonia loss.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied research identifies pyroglutamate formation and ammonia release as important glutamine destruction channels, without complete author/year metadata for the cited decomposition work. The specific kinetic treatment here is therefore speculative. This sink is included to prevent analytical detection in Bizzarri et al. (2026), or the provisional Chimiak et al. (2023) result, from being equated with environmental accumulation.

pathways.name: Strecker-fed Canyon Diablo irradiation route
pathways.description: Prepare DAMN and glycine in parallel from simple feedstocks, combine them with boundary-supplied formamide, and apply the Canyon Diablo irradiation formulation. The final mixture experiment reports glutamine; the complete upstream supply, separation, anoxic compatibility, and transfer sequence has not been demonstrated. This is a conditional integrated route, not a known atom-resolved synthesis.

pathways.name: Strecker-fed NWA 4482 irradiation route
pathways.description: Use the same explicit DAMN/glycine supply chemistry with the separately tested NWA 4482 formulation. Its target endpoint is supported by the reported analytical detection, but its lower crude-residue abundance is not converted into a network yield. This is a mineral-formulation variant of P1, not an independently resolved mechanism.

pathways.name: Strecker-fed Gold Basin irradiation route
pathways.description: Supply DAMN and Strecker-derived glycine to the tested Gold Basin formulation. The reported glutamine abundance is the lowest of the three meteorite systems. Upstream integration and product survival are untested; changing meteorite material does not establish an independent carbon-assembly mechanism.

pathways.name: Mineral-derived glycine feeding Canyon Diablo irradiation
pathways.description: Combine HCN-derived DAMN with glycine made by the peer-reviewed ferroan-brucite nitrate platform, then use the Canyon Diablo formulation. Glycine extraction, neutralization, removal of nitrate/iron residues, concentration, and cold-matrix preparation are necessary unvalidated interfaces. These handling operations are not invented as identity-changing reactions.

pathways.name: Mineral-derived glycine feeding NWA 4482 irradiation
pathways.description: Use the experimentally supported alternative glycine-production platform with the NWA 4482 irradiation formulation. Production of mostly mineral-bound glycine is not equivalent to delivery of the concentrated free glycine used in the irradiation experiment. No end-to-end experiment or natural transport time is established.

pathways.name: Mineral-derived glycine feeding Gold Basin irradiation
pathways.description: Join the ferroan-brucite glycine branch and HCN-derived DAMN preparation to the Gold Basin formulation. This is a distinct graph route using demonstrated component experiments, but their chemical compatibility and geological co-location are not demonstrated. It shares the same unresolved irradiation mechanism as P1–P5.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic precursor route with an explicit terminal gap
pathways.description: Construct the aminodinitrile through cyanoacetylene, maleonitrile, succinonitrile, and aldehyde/cyanohydrin chemistry. Precursor formation has substantial experimental support, but rxn_014 is unresolved. This is not a demonstrated free-glutamine route and cannot be assigned a target yield by multiplying precursor yields.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-derived acrolein route with an explicit terminal gap
pathways.description: Generate low steady-state acrolein from formaldehyde and acetaldehyde, trap it through coupled cyanide additions, and form the common aminodinitrile. Matching dilute upstream production to the concentrated trapping experiment is unproven. Selective free-glutamine production remains blocked by rxn_014.

pathways.name: Discharge-supplied acrolein route with an explicit terminal gap
pathways.description: Use the experimentally precedented discharge source of acrolein instead of aqueous aldehyde condensation, followed by the supported cyanide-capture/aminonitrile chemistry. The displayed discharge source equation is schematic, delivery concentrations are unknown, and the final glutamine-selective hydrolysis is not established. This is an alternative precursor history, not a distinct validated terminal synthesis.

pathways.name: Provisional nitrate–pyruvate ferroan-brucite route
pathways.description: Represent the conference-level report of glutamine formation from pyruvate and nitrate on ferroan brucite without inventing unidentified oligomer structures. Direct product assignment, the proposed carbon-loss mechanism, and the displayed net stoichiometry require independent validation. The peer-reviewed glycine result does not validate this glutamine pathway.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The parallel DAMN and Strecker-glycine preparations provide a coherent assembly plan. Bizzarri et al. (2026), as summarized in the supplied research, directly report glutamine in the Canyon Diablo irradiation formulation. Nevertheless, rxn_005 violates conservation as encoded: no positive coefficient assignment balances the listed reactants against glutamine alone. Its empirical-observation designation appropriately acknowledges uncertainty but does not repair the reaction node. Reported target detection therefore supports chemical accessibility, not a closed stoichiometric pathway or an established environmental throughput.
suggestions: Represent rxn_005 as a non-stoichiometric experimental observation outside the balanced reaction layer until consumed substrates, coproducts, and material exchanges are characterized; do not invent missing products.
Specify the reported irradiation conditions: 170 MeV protons, 6 Gy, 3 minutes, 243 K, and 1 wt% meteorite powder, while separately justifying their environmental analogue.
Quantify precursor recovery, formulation preparation, and glutamine separation and survival rather than treating the crude-residue analytical yield as an end-to-end conversion yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route has credible upstream precursor chemistry and a reported glutamine-positive NWA 4482 formulation in Bizzarri et al. (2026). Its decisive defect is rxn_006, which is UNBALANCED under the supplied ground-truth check. Unknown coproducts prevent interpretation as a conserved synthesis reaction. The different meteorite formulation does not resolve the same mechanistic, mass-balance, and environmental-transfer uncertainties affecting P1. Its reported glutamine abundance is not a molar yield from the boundary feedstocks.
suggestions: Separate the empirical detection record from the stoichiometric network unless a measured input-output balance becomes available.
Attach the NWA 4482-specific formulation, irradiation protocol, analytical identification, and yield normalization directly to rxn_006.
Demonstrate compatibility between recovered Strecker products and the irradiation mixture, including residual water, salts, and competing organics.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied literature reports glutamine detection with Gold Basin material, and the proposed precursor preparations are chemically reasonable. However, rxn_007 cannot conserve atoms using the listed species, regardless of allowed coefficients. The lower reported product abundance does not by itself invalidate detection or justify a different conservation score from P1 and P2. As represented, this remains a supported mixture-to-product observation embedded in an incomplete synthesis model.
suggestions: Retain the Gold Basin result as experimental evidence, but remove its interpretation as a balanced reaction until missing material outputs are established.
Record the actual irradiation conditions and distinguish laboratory dose delivery from a proposed natural exposure history.
Measure glutamine recovery and degradation in the complete product mixture under the proposed separation and storage conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The nitrate/glyoxylate ferroan-brucite platform has peer-reviewed support for glycine production, and rxn_004 is balanceable. The iron nodes can reasonably represent mineral redox inventories; their notation does not require dissolved ferric iron in alkaline water. The unresolved interface is mobilization of mineral-associated glycine into the formamide/DAMN irradiation formulation: the cited study reports that up to 97% of glycine can remain mineral-bound. The terminal rxn_005 additionally violates conservation as encoded.
suggestions: Record the balanced rxn_004 coefficients and specify the actual mineral phase, redox capacity, solution composition, and proton bookkeeping.
Measure environmentally plausible glycine desorption and transfer; analytical recovery by acid digestion is not itself an implemented environmental transfer process.
Replace rxn_005 with a clearly separated empirical observation or a experimentally established complete material balance.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The mineral glycine source and the NWA 4482 glutamine detection each have supporting evidence, but their operational connection has not been demonstrated. Mineral adsorption, desorption, dilution, and formulation preparation determine whether glycine actually reaches the irradiation stage at a useful concentration. Independently, rxn_006 is an unbalanced reaction node. These are integration and conservation limitations, not objections to the selected feedstocks or to using multiple environments.
suggestions: Add a quantitatively justified glycine-release and formulation-preparation operation, including recovery losses and residual mineral or salt effects.
Attach source-specific conditions and citations to both the mineral-production and irradiation records.
Keep rxn_006 outside the conserved reaction layer until its missing coproducts and substrate contributions are experimentally constrained.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a topologically connected combination of demonstrated mineral glycine chemistry and a reported Gold Basin glutamine-positive irradiation experiment. It is not yet an operationally validated sequence because mineral-bound glycine must be recovered and incorporated into the irradiation formulation. Furthermore, rxn_007 has an unavoidable conservation violation with the current species list. The network correctly avoids claiming an independently established mechanism for this formulation variant.
suggestions: Determine the dissolved and mineral-bound glycine fractions and test transfer into the Gold Basin formulation without assuming quantitative recovery.
Resolve the rxn_007 material balance experimentally or preserve it solely as a non-stoichiometric evidence link.
Measure time-dependent glutamine formation and loss after irradiation, including the effects of residual minerals.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Patel et al. (2015) provide strong experimental support for the sequence through the aminodinitrile. All listed reactions are conservation-valid after appropriate coefficients are assigned. The five-carbon precursor formula is consistent with glutamine; the central problem is differential nitrile hydrolysis, not carbon count. Rxn_014 requires conversion of the alpha nitrile to a carboxyl group while stopping the terminal nitrile at the amide, which the supplied literature does not establish as an efficient free-glutamine synthesis. Copper speciation, sulfide compatibility, irradiation conditions, and staged reagent delivery also remain insufficiently specified.
suggestions: Specify mol_024 structurally as N≡C-CH(NH2)-CH2-CH2-C≡N so that the required hydrolysis regioselectivity is explicit.
Experimentally establish rxn_014 with time-resolved identification and quantification of glutamine, glutamate, partially hydrolyzed intermediates, and cyclization products.
Document UV exposure, pH, copper complexes, sulfide delivery, and transfer recoveries for the supported precursor sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aldehyde-derived acrolein source has experimental precedent, and Fernández-García et al. (2017) support the acrolein/cyanide precursor chemistry. Rxn_016 requires two HCN equivalents and is balanceable accordingly. The environmental integration problem is connecting low steady-state acrolein production to conditions comparable to the reported high-yield experiment, approximately 140 mM acrolein and 700 mM cyanide at pH 9.2. Acrolein loss and polymerization compete with capture. Even successful precursor production leaves the shared rxn_014 glutamine-selectivity gap unresolved.
suggestions: Measure coupled acrolein generation and cyanide capture at the concentrations actually attainable in the proposed environment.
Include competing aldehyde reactions, acrolein polymerization, and cyanide availability in the material-throughput assessment.
Do not classify precursor production as glutamine synthesis until rxn_014 is experimentally validated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Discharge production of acrolein has literature precedent, but that does not establish rxn_017 as a measured methane/water-to-acrolein material balance. Its inferred equation is conserved, yet neither the stated hydrogen coproduct stoichiometry nor useful acrolein production under a specified gas mixture and discharge regime is demonstrated here. Capture into an aqueous cyanide stage is also unspecified. The downstream precursor chemistry is supported, but rxn_014 still prevents an established route to free glutamine.
suggestions: Replace the schematic discharge equation with a source-specific experimental production record or a characterized net balance, including actual gas composition and energy input.
Quantify acrolein condensation, trapping, survival, and delivery to the cyanide reaction rather than assuming efficient atmospheric-to-aqueous transfer.
Validate selective aminodinitrile hydrolysis and subsequent glutamine preservation independently of the discharge source.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The 2023 Goldschmidt report supplies provisional direct evidence for glutamine formation from nitrate and pyruvate with ferroan brucite. The later peer-reviewed glycine work supports the mineral platform but does not independently confirm this glutamine result. Rxn_018 is balanceable, including three pyruvates and four CO2 products, but those inferred coefficients do not establish the proposed carbon rearrangement, nitrogen incorporation, or actual coproduct distribution. The mineral setting is plausible; its glutamine-forming mechanism and production-versus-degradation behavior remain insufficiently established.
suggestions: Obtain replicated quantitative glutamine identification with standards and an orthogonal analytical method, measuring both dissolved and mineral-associated product.
Use carbon- and nitrogen-isotope tracing to determine substrate contributions, carbon losses, and whether the proposed CO2-containing net equation is correct.
Specify mineral composition, temperature, pH, redox capacity, concentrations, and time-dependent glutamine formation and degradation.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a connected, adequately populated candidate network with consistent molecule IDs and appropriate five-carbon formulas for glutamine and its aminodinitrile precursor. Parallel precursor preparation is topologically legitimate. The deterministic check establishes that 17 reactions conserve atoms and charge with suitable coefficients, but rxn_005, rxn_006, and rxn_007 are conservation violations as represented. At unit coefficients each has an excess elemental inventory of C2H2N4 on the reactant side; this is not an identified coproduct, and no single common small species repairs the equations. Their explicit empirical labeling is scientifically responsible, but does not make them valid stoichiometric reactions. Missing outputs must be characterized or these records must be separated from the conserved reaction layer. The evidence hierarchy otherwise aligns well with the supplied literature: strong precursor chemistry, reported irradiation-based glutamine detection, an unresolved rxn_014 hydrolysis, and a provisional rxn_018 mineral result. Individual reaction records still need source-linked citations and operating conditions. Surface and Biochemical labels alone do not specify temperature, pH, phase, irradiation, catalyst speciation, or transport. Mineral redox-inventory notation and abbreviated acid-base equilibria are not themselves defects. The coefficients involving S8 likewise reflect its molecular formula rather than an inherently implausible stoichiometry. Rxn_017 and rxn_018 remain hypotheses despite being balanceable. Rxn_019 and rxn_020 are balanced, chemically plausible glutamine-loss channels, but listing them does not establish preservation or net accumulation. Overall confidence is constrained by terminal chemistry and operational integration rather than an average of successful precursor reactions.
